1338.title: At the deathbed
1338.hook: beside the dying, the words la ilaha illallah are said gently, so they can be the last
1338.howItsDone: At a deathbed, Muslim family members gently say la ilaha illallah near the dying person, without pressing them to repeat it, and after death they say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.

segments.voice: Yesterday: remembering death, and your line, remember the end. Today, from remembering the end to standing beside it.

The room is quiet. A machine beeps somewhere, or a clock ticks, or there's only breathing. Family sits close. Someone holds a hand. And at some point, in Muslim homes and hospital rooms, someone leans in near the one who is dying and says, softly, a single line. La ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. Not loudly. Not as a command. Just said near them, so they might hear it, and say it too. It's the line at the heart of the faith, and the hope is that it will be the last they hear and say.
screen: `THE ROOM IS QUIET.` → `SOMEONE LEANS IN.` → `LET IT BE THE LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: The practice comes from a short hadith in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase: prompt your dying ones to say la ilaha illallah. The Arabic word for this prompting is talqin, gently putting words on someone's tongue. And a hadith in Abu Dawud gives the hope behind it: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter the garden. That's why the line is said there. Not as a test the dying person has to pass. As a gift, offered at the door. Some scholars advised doing it with great gentleness: say it near them rather than ordering them to repeat it, and if they say it once, don't keep pressing. The dying are tired; the words are meant to comfort, not to burden. Sahih Muslim keeps another instruction for that room, from Umm Salamah. When you are with the sick or the dying, the Prophet said, in paraphrase, say good things, because the angels say amen to whatever you say. So the words in that room matter. Then, when death comes, there's a line from the Qur'an that Muslims say. In Pickthall's translation of surah al-Baqarah: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." The first line, said beside the bed, is about Allah alone. The line said after is about where the person has gone. Between them, a family keeps its voice low and its words good.
screen: `PROMPT YOUR DYING: LA ILAHA ILLALLAH.` · `TALQIN: GENTLY, NOT PRESSING.` · `SAY GOOD THINGS; ANGELS SAY AMEN.` · `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: Listen to the line, and if you pray, say it with your breath: la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah, slowly and softly, as if to someone you love who is very tired. Then the second line, for after: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning. Say each a few times, quietly, until the words feel familiar in your mouth.
At the deathbed. Saying la ilaha illallah gently near the dying, speaking only good, and afterward, unto Him we are returning. Today's word.
Your line: say it softly to them. A gift at the door, never a test. Softly, then, until tomorrow.

1339.title: Washing the body
1339.hook: the Prophet's instructions to the women washing his daughter: water and lote leaves, the right side first, camphor at the end
1339.howItsDone: After a death, Muslims wash the body (ghusl), usually by family members or trained community volunteers of the same sex, keeping it covered, washing an odd number of times with water and often lote leaves, and adding camphor at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: at the deathbed, and your line, say it softly to them. Today, the first thing done after death: the washing.

Women are washing a young woman's body when her father comes into the room. That's how a report in Sahih al-Bukhari begins, told by one of the women, Umm 'Atiyyah. The father is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his daughter has died. He doesn't take over. He doesn't make a speech. He gives them instructions, quiet and practical, the kind you'd give someone you trust with something precious. And when they finish, he hands them something of his own.
screen: `A FATHER WALKS IN.` → `QUIET, PRACTICAL INSTRUCTIONS.` → `SOMETHING OF HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's what he told them, in paraphrase from al-Bukhari. Wash her three times, or five, or more if you see the need, with water and sidr, the leaves of the lote tree. Put camphor in the last washing. Begin with her right side, and with the places washed in wudu. Then tell me when you've finished. Notice the tenderness in it. The order follows the washing a person does before prayer, and some readers hear in it a last preparation, as if to stand before Allah. The lote leaves and the camphor bring cleanness and fragrance. And the count is left open, as many times as care requires. When they finished and told him, Umm 'Atiyyah says, he gave them his own waist-wrap and told them to wrap her in it, next to her body. A father's garment, the last thing she wore against her skin. That's the root of a practice that continues. The washing is called ghusl. It's done by family, or by people from the community who have learned how, usually people of the same sex as the one who died. The body is kept covered while it's washed, and handled slowly, gently, as if the person could still feel it. Some who do this work describe it as an honor. The person on the table can't thank them, can't return the favor, can't even know, and some say that's part of what makes it pure. Dignity, here, isn't something the dead have to earn. It's something the living give.
screen: `THREE, OR FIVE, OR MORE.` · `THE RIGHT SIDE AND THE PLACES OF WUDU.` · `HIS OWN WAIST-WRAP.` · `DIGNITY THE LIVING GIVE.`

segments.voice: This may be tender, so go gently. Think of someone you've lost, or of the people who care for the dead in any community, and picture careful hands, a covered body, water poured slowly; notice the respect in it. If you pray, remember those who have died. And if grief ever feels like too much to carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
Washing the body. Ghusl for the one who has died: water and lote leaves, the right side first, camphor last, and the body kept covered and handled gently. Today's word.
Your line: washed with care. Gentle hands, for someone who can't say thank you. Thank you for staying with a tender day.

1340.title: The shroud
1340.hook: plain white cloth, the same for the rich and the poor
1340.howItsDone: After the washing, Muslims wrap the body in a kafan of plain white cloth, kept simple whatever the person's wealth; a pilgrim who dies in ihram may be shrouded in the ihram garments.

segments.voice: Yesterday: washing the body, and your line, washed with care. Today, after the washing, the wrapping.

How was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, dressed for his burial? 'A'ishah answers in Sahih al-Bukhari, and the answer is almost nothing. Three white sheets of Yemeni cotton. No shirt among them. No turban. The man his followers called the Messenger of Allah, wrapped in plain cloth, the way anyone could be. No embroidery, no rank, no sign of who he'd been. Just cloth, and the body inside it. Today's word is that cloth.
screen: `HOW WAS HE DRESSED FOR BURIAL?` → `THREE WHITE SHEETS.` → `NO SHIRT, NO TURBAN.`

segments.voice: The word is kafan, the shroud. A hadith in Abu Dawud gives the color, in paraphrase: wear white, for it's among the best of your clothes, and shroud your dead in it. So the custom is plain white cloth, wrapped around the washed body, the same whether the person owned a palace or a single room. Two more reports show what that can mean. In al-Bukhari, a man on pilgrimage was thrown from his camel at 'Arafah and killed, still wearing the two plain cloths of ihram. The Prophet said, in paraphrase: wash him with water and lote leaves, and shroud him in his two garments. Don't perfume him, and don't cover his head, for he will be raised on the Day of Rising saying the pilgrim's call. His pilgrim's clothes became his shroud. And from Khabbab, also in al-Bukhari, the story of Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, killed at the battle of Uhud. All he left was one cloak. When they covered his head with it, his feet showed. When they covered his feet, his head showed. The Prophet told them to cover his head, and lay a sweet-smelling grass, idhkhir, over his feet. Not enough cloth, and still enough honor. Put those beside the three white sheets, and some readers hear the shroud saying something: that the things that separated people in life, the clothes, the labels, the bank balance, stay behind. What goes into the earth is wrapped in the same white.
screen: `KAFAN: THE SHROUD.` · `WEAR WHITE, SHROUD YOUR DEAD IN IT.` · `A PILGRIM IN HIS TWO CLOTHS.` · `ONE CLOAK, NOT ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Look down at what you're wearing, and think of the things you own that say something about you: a watch, a brand, a title on a badge, a car. Let each one fall away in your mind until there's only you, wrapped in something plain and white, and notice what's still there when the labels are gone. If you pray, rest in that plainness before Allah.
Kafan. The shroud: plain white cloth, the same for anyone, rich or poor. Today's word.

1341.title: The funeral prayer
1341.hook: a prayer said standing, with no bowing and no prostration, and a duty on the whole community
1341.howItsDone: Muslims pray salat al-janazah standing in rows behind the body, with four takbirs and no bowing or prostration, usually reciting al-Fatiha, blessings on the Prophet and a du'a for the deceased; the schools differ on some details.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kafan, the shroud, and your line, everyone in white. Today, the community stands before the one in white.

After a regular prayer at the mosque, sometimes the imam turns and says a few quiet words, and people who came only for the noon prayer stay standing. A body, wrapped in white, has been placed at the front. Rows form behind it. And then comes a prayer unlike the others of the day. Nobody bows. Nobody goes down to the ground. The whole prayer happens standing up, and it's over in a few minutes. Some in those rows never met the person, and they are praying for them now.
screen: `A BODY AT THE FRONT.` → `ROWS FORM BEHIND IT.` → `NOBODY BOWS. NOBODY KNEELS.`

segments.voice: It's called salat al-janazah, the funeral prayer. Al-Bukhari keeps a report that shows its shape. When the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, died far away, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, announced his death to the people on the very day it happened. He went out with them to the place of prayer, lined them up in rows, and said Allahu akbar four times. That's the frame: standing, in rows, with four takbirs. In common practice, between them come the opening of the Qur'an, blessings on the Prophet, and du'a for the one who has died, though the schools of law differ on some details. Al-Bukhari also reports that Ibn 'Abbas recited al-Fatiha in a funeral prayer and said he did it so people would know it was the sunnah. Why standing only? One reading is simple: the prayer is for someone else. You stand before Allah on another person's behalf, asking mercy for them. The jurists call it fard kifayah, a communal duty. If some of the community do it, the duty is lifted from the rest; if nobody does, the whole community is at fault. And there's a reward for whoever shows up. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet said, in paraphrase: whoever attends a funeral until the prayer has a qirat, and whoever stays until the burial has two. Someone asked what two qirats were. Like two huge mountains, he said. The person in white can't ask. The community stands for them.
screen: `FOUR TAKBIRS, STANDING, IN ROWS.` · `FATIHA, BLESSINGS, AND DU'A.` · `A COMMUNAL DUTY.` · `TWO QIRATS, LIKE TWO MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you're able, feet planted, hands still, and feel what it's like to stand without any other movement. Think of someone who has died, someone you knew or a stranger whose name you heard, and stay standing for them for a few breaths. If you pray, ask mercy for them in your own words.
Salat al-janazah. The funeral prayer: said standing, with four takbirs, no bowing, a duty the community carries together. Today's word.
Your line: stand for them. Two mountains, for a few minutes on your feet. Peace to you, until tomorrow.

1342.title: Burial facing the qiblah
1342.hook: quickly, facing the qiblah, in the earth
1342.howItsDone: Muslims bury the dead soon after death, in the earth, wrapped in the shroud and laid on the right side facing the qiblah; mourners help fill the grave, and some communities recite Qur'an 20:55 as they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salat al-janazah: the funeral prayer, said standing, a duty the community carries together. Today, the walk from the prayer to the grave.

A burial in the Qur'an begins in the worst way. In surah al-Ma'idah, one of Adam's two sons has killed his brother, and he stands there with the body and no idea what to do with it. Then Allah sends a raven. The bird scratches at the ground, digging, and the killer watches. He cries out in shame, in paraphrase, that he couldn't even manage what this raven manages: to cover his brother. So a grave in the Qur'an is dug by someone learning from a bird.
screen: `A BODY, AND NO IDEA WHAT TO DO.` → `A RAVEN SCRATCHES THE GROUND.` → `A GRAVE, LEARNED FROM A BIRD.`

segments.voice: Start with the speed. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells people to hurry with the funeral. His reasoning, in paraphrase: if the one who died was good, you're bringing them toward good; if not, it's a weight you set down from your shoulders. So the washing, the shroud and the prayer come quickly, and the burial follows close behind. Grief doesn't get to wait for everything to be perfect. Then the direction. Every day of a Muslim's life, the prayer faced one place: the qiblah, toward the Ka'bah in Makkah. In the grave, as the jurists describe it, the body is laid on its right side, the face turned that same way. A whole life of turning one way, and it doesn't stop at the end. And then the earth. Muslim burial is in the ground itself, plainly, in the white shroud, and mourners may help fill the grave by hand. Some communities recite a verse from surah Ta Ha at that moment, in Pickthall's translation: "Thereof We created you, and thereunto We return you, and thence We bring you forth a second time." From the earth, back to the earth, out of it again. In the verse, the ground isn't the end of the sentence. It's the comma.
screen: `HURRY WITH THE FUNERAL.` · `FACING THE QIBLAH, EVEN NOW.` · `INTO THE EARTH, BY HAND.` · `FROM IT, TO IT, OUT OF IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Let your weight settle into the chair or the floor, and notice the ground holding you up, as it has every day of your life without being asked. If you pray, you can remember someone who has already been returned to the earth.

1343.title: Three days
1343.hook: mourning is three days, and a widow's waiting period is longer (Bukhari)
1343.howItsDone: Muslims observe a period of mourning for a relative, which a hadith in al-Bukhari limits to three days, while a widow keeps a longer waiting period, the 'iddah, described in Qur'an 2:234

segments.voice: Yesterday, the burial: quickly, on the right side, facing the qiblah, back to the earth. Today, the people walking home from the grave.

News came to Umm Habibah, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: her father had died. She waited. On the third day, she called for perfume, a yellowish scent, and rubbed some on her arms and face. Then she explained, in paraphrase: I have no need of perfume. But I heard the Prophet say that a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not mourn anyone more than three days, except a husband. Zaynab bint Abi Salamah tells it, in Sahih al-Bukhari. A daughter who has just lost her father, putting on perfume, on purpose.
screen: `NEWS OF HER FATHER.` → `ON THE THIRD DAY, PERFUME.` → `I HAVE NO NEED OF IT.`

segments.voice: The perfume was a signal: the outward mourning is finished. The hadith speaks to a believing woman. For three days, grief is given room, and adornment like perfume is set aside. Then, by the Prophet's word, that outward season closes. Umm Habibah wasn't saying she'd stopped missing her father; she said plainly she had no need of the perfume. She was honoring the limit. So there's permission here: grief gets real time, and three days is not a moment. And there's a boundary: the formal mourning doesn't swallow a life whole. The hadith names one exception, a widow, and the Qur'an gives that waiting its own measure. In surah al-Baqarah, women whose husbands have died wait, keeping to themselves, four months and ten days, and then, the verse says, there's no blame on them for what they decide for themselves in a fitting way. That period is the 'iddah. Some readers see it as longer because more has ended: a household, a marriage, a whole shape of life. So there are two clocks, a short one for a relative and a longer one for the person whose life was most rearranged. Neither says the love has stopped. They give grief a container, with a beginning, a middle and a door out, and the people around know when to come close and when to let the grieving rise.

1344.title: Food for the bereaved
1344.hook: make food for the family of Ja'far, for what has come to them (Abu Dawud)
1344.howItsDone: Muslim neighbors and relatives bring meals to a bereaved household in the first days after a death, following the hadith in Abu Dawud about the family of Ja'far, so the family doesn't have to cook or host.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three days: Umm Habibah's perfume, and grief given real time, with a door out. Today, a pot on the stove.

A casserole dish with masking tape on the bottom and a name in marker. A tray of rice left on a doorstep. A neighbor who doesn't knock, just texts: it's outside. Some grieving households end up with a kitchen full of other people's cooking. In Islam, that habit has a sentence behind it, and a name: Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin. When news of his death reached Madinah, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, didn't give a speech. He gave an instruction about dinner.
screen: `A DISH WITH A NAME ON THE BOTTOM.` → `NEWS OF JA'FAR.` → `AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT DINNER.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, told by Ja'far's son 'Abdullah. The Prophet said, in paraphrase: make food for the family of Ja'far, for something has come to them that keeps them busy. Look at the reason. Not that they're sad, though they were. That they're occupied. A death takes over a household: the washing, the shroud, the prayer, the burial, the visitors, the phone calls, the children who need explaining to. Nobody in that house is thinking about lunch, and somebody has to. So the instruction lands on the neighbors, not the family. Jurists later drew a quiet lesson from the same hadith: the burden runs one way. The neighbors cook for the bereaved household, and the household isn't put to the work and expense of feeding a crowd. Now look back over the week. Gentle words at the deathbed. The body washed with care. Everyone in the same white shroud. The community standing in prayer. The grave, facing the qiblah. Three days with a door out. And now a pot of food carried across the street. Much of it is done with hands and feet rather than speeches: washing, wrapping, standing, digging, cooking. In these texts, much of the way through a death is a list of tasks, done for someone who can't do them right now.
